items.text: The 2 most important skills for entry-level workers in the age of AI, says IBM’s chief talent officer
items.article: Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent officer, says college students and entry-level workers need these two skills to succeed as AI reshapes their work. As AI reshapes how people work, particularly along the lowest rungs of the career ladder , many college students and entry-level workers are left wondering what skills will carry them furthest. Two skills in particular are important to develop right now, if you ask Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent, leadership & culture officer. Entry-level workers "have to be focused on ensuring that they are actually building critical thinking [and] judgment," Nair tells CNBC Make It. "There are some things that are going to rapidly change, and some things that humans, only, can do today, which is where they need to double down." In an IBM survey of 1,500 chief human resources officers and 8,800 employees worldwide published in September, roughly 57% of CHROs considered critical thinking an important skill in the AI era, compared to 49% of employees. Approximately 48% of CHROs consider judgment under uncertainty and ambiguity an important skill, compared to just 29% of employees. "Traditionally people were building judgment through actually doing the work," Nair says. "Today, that piece of work is no longer there because AI is doing it." Instead, "actually validating the inputs of AI," Nair says, "helps them build their judgment."

items.article: A former Meta executive who worked closely with Mark Zuckerberg says one lesson from his time at Facebook changed how he thinks about work, leadership and the value of time. Working long hours may seem like part of building a successful company, but former Meta executive Martin Ott says his time working with Mark Zuckerberg taught him a different approach. Ott, who is now the CEO of Berlin-based tax platform Taxfix, says leaders should focus on the work that matters most instead of trying to stay busy all day. Taxfix is valued at more than $1 billion. Ott joined Facebook in 2012 as managing director for Northern and Central Europe. The company was still private at the time and was moving from desktop use to mobile, with only a few thousand employees around the world. Speaking to Fortune, Ott said one of the key lessons he took from working under Zuckerberg was that time is limited and should be used carefully. “There’s only so many hours in a day," Ott said. Ott Says Leaders Should Focus On One Key Task Rather than filling the day with meetings and tasks, Ott believes leaders should think about what could have the biggest effect on the business. “Ask yourself, what is the real one thing you could do today to really have impact, make a difference?" he said. He also suggested that employees and managers should think twice before joining every meeting on their calendars. According to Ott, spending more hours at work does not always mean creating more value.

Protein has become a major focus in conversations about fitness, weight management, and healthy ageing. But how much do you actually need every day? And does everyone need the same amount? According to Dt Amreen Sheikh, Chief Dietician, KIMS Hospitals, Thane, protein requirements are primarily calculated based on body weight, but several other factors can influence an individual’s needs. “For a healthy adult, the ICMR-NIN recommendation is about 0.83 g of protein per kg of body weight each day,” said Sheikh. For example, a person weighing 60 kg would need approximately 50 g of protein a day based on this recommendation. However, this is not a one-size-fits-all number. “Factors such as age, body weight, level of physical activity and life stage can affect personal protein needs,” Sheikh explained. People who exercise regularly, older adults and those trying to preserve muscle mass may require more protein than a sedentary adult. items.article: Nauru is the only nation to have never played an official international football match and hardly anyone there plays the game. Is that about to change? The country that doesn't play football... yet Like everywhere, the world's smallest island nation has been gripped by football fever for the past six weeks. But once Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday, almost every trace of football on Nauru stopped. Football is almost non-existent on this Pacific island. Nauru has never fielded a team in an official international match and it has just one – hard sand – pitch. While there is interest in big Premier League matches, and children wear Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo kits, any attempts to actually play football tend to be mocked, unless it's Aussie rules. But things may be slowly changing as a group of volunteers - led by British former academy player Charlie Pomroy - seek to introduce the game to what was once the world's richest nation per capita but is now heavily reliant on foreign aid and has one of the highest obesity rates in the world. A social media post from the Nauru Soccer Federation congratulating the new world champions and setting out a dream that "one day we hope to be in Spain's position" may have been fanciful, but the groundwork is real in what it says is the last country not to have had a senior international side.
